The Eastern spadefoot toad, Pelobates syriacus, exhibits a life history closely tied to ephemeral ponds in arid and semi-arid landscapes of the Levant. Field surveys in Israel indicate that newly hatched tadpoles emerge from egg masses at an exceptionally small size, with individual wet weight at birth recorded as 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams]. This minute starting mass is typical of explosive breeders that produce large clutches of small, yolk-rich ova. The developmental trajectory from hatching to the initiation of metamorphosis is tightly constrained by pond hydroperiod. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the larval period from hatching to metamorphic climax spans approximately 120 days , a relatively protracted duration for a species that breeds in temporary waters. This extended larval phase likely reflects the energetic demands of reaching the size threshold for metamorphosis, which is observed at a snout-vent length of 2.9 centimeters  shortly before tail resorption is complete.

Sexual maturation in Pelobates syriacus is achieved after a substantial period of post-metamorphic growth, with distinct trajectories between the sexes. Following the transition to terrestrial life, females require approximately 3.2 years since metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3.2 years since metamorphosis] to attain puberty under a thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Males, by contrast, mature slightly later, reaching sexual maturity at roughly 3.5 years since metamorphosis [tp = roughly 3.5 years since metamorphosis] under identical conditions at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This difference appears counterintuitive in a species where males typically mature earlier, but it may be linked to the higher energetic cost of producing the larger gonadal mass required for amplexus and fertilization. The body size at which these pubertal milestones are crossed also differs: females achieve a snout-vent length of 6.3 centimeters [Lp = 6.3 centimeters] at the onset of reproductive capacity, whereas males are slightly more diminutive at this stage, measuring 6.2 centimeters [Lp = 6.2 centimeters] in SVL.

Adult body mass in Pelobates syriacus shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a substantially larger ultimate wet weight than males. The maximum recorded wet weight for adult females reaches 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams], more than 30 percent heavier than the ultimate wet weight for males, which peaks at 90 grams [Wwi = 90 grams]. This disparity is partly explained by the energetic demands of egg production, as gravid females carry large, water-laden egg masses. At the onset of sexual maturity, the wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 40 grams [Wwp = approximately 40 grams], while males reach the same developmental stage at a lower body mass of 25.8 grams [Wwp = 25.8 grams]. This pattern of a larger female body mass threshold for maturation is consistent with fecundity selection, where larger body size directly increases clutch volume and thereby reproductive output.

Reproductive output in this species is high, reflecting its adaptation to unpredictable breeding environments. Although direct estimates of annual fecundity in the wild are scarce, field observations near breeding ponds during the rainy season suggest that a single female can produce between 16 and 17 eggs per day [Ri = between 16 and 17 eggs per day] during the peak of the breeding window. This rate translates to roughly 6000 eggs per year , a figure that must be contextualized by the ephemeral nature of available water bodies. The actual number of spawning nights per season is considerably lower, but the potential maximum reproductive rate under ideal conditions is nonetheless substantial. This prodigious output is a classic bet-hedging strategy, compensating for high larval mortality caused by pond desiccation before metamorphosis is completed.

Longevity in Pelobates syriacus is moderate for anuran amphibians of its body size. The maximum recorded lifespan under field conditions, based on mark-recapture studies of a population in northern Israel, is 15 years [am = 15 years], though most individuals in the wild likely succumb earlier to predation or habitat desiccation at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The age at hatching, measured as the incubation period from oviposition to larval eclosion, is brief: at a constant temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], embryos hatch after approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days], a rapid onset that accelerates entry into the larval stage. Furthermore, adult body size continues to increase throughout life, with the ultimate snout-vent length for females reaching 10.6 centimeters [Li = 10.6 centimeters], distinctly larger than the ultimate snout-vent length for males, which attains 9.3 centimeters [Li = 9.3 centimeters]. These asymptotic dimensions underscore the profound sexual size dimorphism that characterizes this fossorial specialist.
